Datadog Jumps 5% as Bernstein Upgrade Cites AI Demand; Snowflake Rises 3%, Cloudflare Holds Steady
Bernstein just reversed its Datadog call one quarter after a downgrade shook the stock, pointing to AI token consumption as the reason. Whether that optimism survives the November earnings report is the question every investor in the space should be…
Published October 19, 2026, 10:47am ET · 3 min read
Market Movers desk. Editor: David Moadel.
Amidst glowing server racks, a technician manages the critical AI infrastructure that underpins the 'neocloud' services discussed in the article, highlighting the intense competition between companies like CoreWeave and Nebius. © baranozdemir / Getty Images
Signs of accelerating AI workloads are pulling cloud software back into favor after a rough stretch for technology names. Datadog (NASDAQ:DDOG | DDOG Price Prediction) stock is up 5% to $259.15 in morning trading, leading the group higher.
Bernstein upgraded Datadog stock to Outperform from Market Perform, stating that its data show enterprise AI token consumption at the largest AI labs growing rapidly quarter over quarter. The new rating rests on the conclusion that the earlier view of Datadog’s AI-driven growth was too conservative, a reversal that comes one quarter after a downgrade tied to a revenue cut at Datadog’s largest AI-native customer and slower demand among established clients.
A broad selloff in technology stocks the prior week sets the background for the upgrade. Observability software from Datadog tracks how applications and cloud infrastructure perform, so more AI tokens moving through customer systems could translate into more activity for the company to monitor and bill.
Second-quarter 2026 results already gave Datadog’s AI story a solid base. The company posted revenue of $1.12 billion, up 35.6% from a year earlier, and non-GAAP earnings per share (EPS) of $0.65, beating expectations. That marked Datadog’s fifth consecutive EPS beat.
Datadog’s larger accounts kept expanding as well, with customers paying $100,000 or more in annual recurring revenue up 23% to approximately 4,720. Growth in that tier picked up from 21% in the first quarter of 2026.
Management raised Datadog’s full-year 2026 revenue guidance to between $4.45 billion and $4.47 billion after that report. Chief executive Olivier Pomel tied the momentum to AI. He made the point in the August release, stating, “Our customers are building and deploying with AI, and they are using the Datadog platform to observe, secure, and act on their AI-enabled solutions.”
Datadog has been shipping products aimed directly at AI customers, including Bits AI for autonomous incident detection and resolution, AI Guard for protecting AI agents, and Bits Agent Builder for creating custom agents. The company launched more than 100 new capabilities at its DASH 2026 conference, including a Bring Your Own Cloud model that runs Datadog inside customer environments. It also acquired Adaptive ML to speed up its AI research.
That product push came alongside better profitability, with Datadog’s non-GAAP operating margin expanding to 23% from 20% a year earlier. Its free cash flow margin reached 25% in the quarter.
Snowflake and Cloudflare Trail the Leader
Checking in on the peers, Snowflake (NYSE:SNOW) stock is up 3%, a solid gain that still trails the jump in Datadog stock. Cloudflare (NYSE:NET) stock is up 0.4% to $297.58, lagging both Datadog stock and Snowflake stock. Snowflake sells a cloud data platform, while Cloudflare runs a network for security and content delivery.
Sector-wide gains are more modest, as the WisdomTree Cloud Computing Fund (NASDAQ:WCLD) is up 0.8%. Broader tech is running ahead of cloud software, as the Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ) is up 1%. That gap leaves the jump in Datadog stock looking like a company-specific reaction to the upgrade.
Bernstein Upgrade Sets Up Datadog’s November Report
Datadog is scheduled to report third-quarter 2026 results in early November, with its guidance calling for revenue of $1.135 billion to $1.145 billion. Datadog’s report needs to show AI-native customers spending more, since the upgrade rests on AI workload growth. Another focus is whether established customers also step up their spending after the slower demand behind last quarter’s downgrade.
Last quarter’s downgrade is a reminder that Datadog’s growth depends partly on its largest AI-native customer. When all is said and done, investors should keep their Datadog stock positions moderate. A second revenue cut could undo the optimism behind the new rating, and the prior week’s tech selloff showed how quickly sentiment can turn.

Published October 16, 2026, 11:54am ET · 3 min read
Market Movers desk. Editor: David Moadel.
Cloud software stocks are under heavy pressure as worries about AI financing spread across the sector. High-growth names that posted strong recent results are absorbing much of the selling.
Snowflake (NYSE:SNOW | SNOW Price Prediction) stock is down 7% at $310.83 early in the session, leading the cloud group lower. Likewise, Cloudflare (NYSE:NET) stock is down 7% to $293.45. Meanwhile, Datadog (NASDAQ:DDOG) stock is down 6% to $249.08, representing a slightly smaller decline than its peers.
Sector funds are falling far less. The First Trust Cloud Computing ETF (NASDAQ:SKYY) is down 4%, while the Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ) is down 1.35%. In other words, large-cap tech is slipping but cloud-computing stocks are generally declining faster.
AI Financing Fears Hit High-Growth Cloud Names
This decline extends a rotation out of AI-linked stocks as investors question how AI infrastructure spending gets financed. Snowflake added its own wrinkle in late September, when it proposed a convertible note offering. Those notes can later convert into equity, placing Snowflake directly inside the financing debate.
Each company sells a different piece of the cloud: Snowflake offers a data platform, Cloudflare runs a global network for security and content delivery, and Datadog sells software that tracks applications and infrastructure. That mix ties revenue at all three to cloud usage, so an AI spending pullback could hit them at once (we featured seven suppliers supporting the AI expansion, from power to networking, in a free report you can grab here).
Strong Earnings Haven’t Shielded Snowflake
Snowflake’s latest results were strong. In its Q2 FY2027 report on September 2, Snowflake posted revenue of $1.55 billion, up 35.1% year over year, along with non-GAAP EPS of $0.62 that beat estimates.
Management also raised Snowflake’s fiscal 2027 product revenue guidance to $6.07 billion from $5.84 billion. Its net revenue retention held at 126%, and remaining performance obligations reached $9 billion. Those figures suggest customers are expanding their commitments to the platform.
AI adoption is adding to Snowflake’s momentum. CoCo passed 9,100 accounts in the quarter, while CoWork expanded to 5,800 accounts. Executives called AI a “powerful flywheel” for consumption.
One concern surfaced on Snowflake’s September earnings call. The company cut its fiscal 2027 non-GAAP product gross margin guidance to 74% because fast-growing AI workloads carry a lower contribution margin. Then-CEO Sridhar Ramaswamy stated “As models have gotten more powerful, cost has absolutely become a concern.”
Cloudflare Steers Clear of the AI Capex Race
Cloudflare has taken a more selective path on AI spending, even as it restructures around what it calls an “agentic AI-first operating model.” On its Q2 2026 earnings call in August, then-CEO Matthew Prince explained why Cloudflare avoids selling commodity compute:
I think not all revenue is created equal. And if you’re selling what is just commodity compute, if you’re basically letting, you know, an AI company use your balance sheet and your credit rating in order to buy servers that are the same as everybody else’s servers, that’s just not attractive business for us.
Prince added that Cloudflare has “always focused on how we can squeeze as much out of every CapEx dollar as possible.” That sets Cloudflare apart from hyperscalers that buy servers and lease them back.
Yet, that discipline hasn’t insulated Cloudflare stock. Datadog has leaned into AI with launches such as Bits AI and AI Guard, and Datadog shares are doing slightly better, though still trailing the cloud ETF.
Snowflake’s Financing Question Hangs Over Cloud Names
Snowflake’s bull case rests on demand for data platforms that feed AI workloads, backed by three straight quarters of accelerating product revenue growth. Cloudflare bulls point to its capital discipline, and Datadog bulls to AI monitoring demand. The bear case for all three: investors keep marking down AI-linked names until financing concerns ease.
The next test for Snowflake is whether AI demand keeps product revenue growth on its guided path. Traders may want to check for whether SKYY closes its gap with QQQ.
Strong recent results give Snowflake, Cloudflare, and Datadog a fundamental buffer, while the financing concern could keep the three stocks volatile. Position sizes should be kept small, if you choose to invest at all, until the AI financing question resolves.

At Goldman Sachs' Communacopia + Technology Conference on September 10, CFO David Obstler pointed to how little of the market has moved. "The research companies say that somewhere upper 20s, 30% of applications are in the cloud," he said. He added that many enterprises "really haven't even started their first material projects." To catch those projects, salespeople in Datadog's key accounts group now cover one or two accounts "where the IT budget and conversion to the cloud can be in the tens of millions." On the in-house question, Obstler described AI-native customers moving the other way: "we're seeing a movement from open source or initial efforts or cobbling it together towards Datadog."
Customers with $100,000 or more in annual recurring revenue reached about 4,720 at the end of the second quarter, up 23% from a year earlier. Obstler called these enterprise sales cycles very long, so that count tracks the strategy better than any single quarter's revenue.
Datadog Trades at Twice the Peer Median on Revenue
At the October 16 close, Datadog's enterprise value traded at around 17 times NTM revenue. The median for the nine companies in TIKR's software comparison set, which runs from Microsoft (MSFT) to RingCentral (RNG), was around 8 times. The October 19 gain pushed Datadog's multiple higher.
Margins support part of that premium. Datadog's second-quarter adjusted EBIT margin widened 307 basis points year over year to 22.92%, while revenue grew 35.64%.
The known gap is the largest customer. Datadog said in August that the account had renewed but that its usage would decline starting in the third quarter, a cut built into guidance. Obstler did not claim every customer stays fully on the platform: "it isn't the case all the time, and it also isn't 100% or 0%." Before Bernstein's upgrade, TIKR's October 16 data showed a mean target of around $290, with 33 Buys, 10 Outperforms, 3 Holds, 1 Underperform, and 1 Sell.
The TIKR model's mid case values Datadog at around $726 by December 31, 2030, a total return of around 179% from $260.36, or around 28% a year over 4.2 years. It is a scenario built on assumptions, not a forecast.
Over the model's 2025 to 2035 forecast, the mid case assumes around 21% annual revenue growth and a net income margin near 29%, against 24.4% over the past year on the model card. The primary risk is a valuation reset toward the peer median before those margins arrive.
On the upside, adjusted margins are already widening. On the downside, a multiple at the peer median of around 8 times revenue would be less than half of Datadog's October 16 level.
November 4 shows whether AI-native customers keep moving onto Datadog, as Obstler described, or in-house, as Bernstein warned. Growth in $100,000-plus customers at or above the second quarter's 23% pace would support the premium. A slowdown below 20% would make the gap to the peer median harder to defend.

Datadog has delivered a powerful run for shareholders over the past few years, which now puts a spotlight on a simple question for anyone looking at the stock today. Do the company's underlying cash flows support a share price that has moved this far, this fast?
Over the past 3 years, Datadog has returned 203.4%. This raises the stakes on whether its current valuation can still be explained by the cash the business is expected to generate.

The long range projections climb into multiple billions of dollars per year, which means a large portion of the estimated worth comes from what Datadog might earn well into the 2030s rather than from current profits. That kind of growth path leaves the valuation sensitive to changes in assumptions about adoption of newer products, including AI driven tools and the push into DevSecOps. Despite the recent rally and insider selling linked to preset trading plans, the DCF output still places Datadog's estimated intrinsic value modestly above the current share price of $271.34, which suggests that the market has not fully closed that gap yet. Datadog Soars 6% on Bernstein Upgrade as AI Token Use Has "Grown at Least 50%" ©@jittawit21 from jittawit21 via Canva, @KanawatTH via Canva
Datadog shares rose 6% today after Bernstein upgraded the stock to Outperform and raised its price target to $350 from $237.
Bernstein's case for faster AI-driven growth looks well-founded, but the stock already prices in a lot of it.
Analysts expect revenue to grow about 30% this year, then slow to about 23% a year through 2028.
Third-quarter results on Nov. 4 are the first real test of whether AI-native customers can make up for slower traditional customers.
Datadog (DDOG:NASDAQ) shares are up 6% today. Before the open, Bernstein upgraded the stock to Outperform from Market Perform and raised its price target to $350 from $237.
The bounce follows a drop of about 14% last week in a broad tech selloff.
It's quite the reversal. Bernstein downgraded Datadog last quarter for two reasons. Its largest "Born in AI" customer (widely reported to be OpenAI) cut about $100 million of annual recurring revenue. And demand looked softer among the traditional customers that make up around 85% of revenue. At the time, Bernstein expected growth from AI-native customers to slow to 50%-60% in 2027, from 80%-90% this year.
Now Bernstein analyst Peter Weed says that view was too conservative:
"Our alt data signals suggest enterprise token consumption appears to have grown at least 50% [quarter over quarter] among the largest AI Labs (and perhaps even faster in their smaller 'Born in AI' customers)."
He added that consumer AI agents like Muse and Dots could raise the monitoring needs of Datadog's traditional customers too.
Wall Street's estimates already have Datadog growing fast for years…
Datadog (DDOG): revenue, actual and consensus estimates, $ billions, fiscal 2023–2028 (TIKR)
Consensus has revenue climbing about 30% this year to $4.47 billion, then slowing to about 23% a year, reaching $6.78 billion in 2028. Bernstein is betting against that slowdown. If the biggest AI labs keep adding usage at anything like 50% a quarter, those later years look conservative to me.
Of course, more tokens don't turn straight into Datadog revenue. And Weed himself points out that customers who get big enough have tended to move monitoring in-house.
Shares were up about 82% this year through Friday's close, and the valuation has followed…
Datadog (DDOG): forward (NTM) P/E, last 5 years (TIKR)
At Friday's close, Datadog traded at 93.2x forward earnings, and after today's jump it's closer to 99x. That's under its five-year average of 107.6x, which the 2021 bubble pushed up. But it's about double the 47.4x the stock hit in February.
My take: Bernstein's upgrade looks well-founded. If AI-native customers keep growing like this, Datadog's revenue should beat what the Street expects for 2027 and 2028.
But at nearly 100x forward earnings, the stock needs proof. Datadog reports third-quarter results on Nov. 4. That will be the first real look at whether its AI-native customers are making up for any slowdown among its traditional ones.

Cloud software stocks are under heavy pressure as worries about AI financing spread across the sector. High-growth names that posted strong recent results are absorbing much of the selling.
Snowflake (NYSE:SNOW | SNOW Price Prediction) stock is down 7% at $310.83 early in the session, leading the cloud group lower. Likewise, Cloudflare (NYSE:NET) stock is down 7% to $293.45. Meanwhile, Datadog (NASDAQ:DDOG) stock is down 6% to $249.08, representing a slightly smaller decline than its peers.
Sector funds are falling far less. The First Trust Cloud Computing ETF (NASDAQ:SKYY) is down 4%, while the Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ) is down 1.35%. In other words, large-cap tech is slipping but cloud-computing stocks are generally declining faster.
AI Financing Fears Hit High-Growth Cloud Names
This decline extends a rotation out of AI-linked stocks as investors question how AI infrastructure spending gets financed. Snowflake added its own wrinkle in late September, when it proposed a convertible note offering. Those notes can later convert into equity, placing Snowflake directly inside the financing debate.
Each company sells a different piece of the cloud: Snowflake offers a data platform, Cloudflare runs a global network for security and content delivery, and Datadog sells software that tracks applications and infrastructure. That mix ties revenue at all three to cloud usage, so an AI spending pullback could hit them at once (we featured seven suppliers supporting the AI expansion, from power to networking, in a free report you can grab here).
Strong Earnings Haven’t Shielded Snowflake
Snowflake’s latest results were strong. In its Q2 FY2027 report on September 2, Snowflake posted revenue of $1.55 billion, up 35.1% year over year, along with non-GAAP EPS of $0.62 that beat estimates.
Management also raised Snowflake’s fiscal 2027 product revenue guidance to $6.07 billion from $5.84 billion. Its net revenue retention held at 126%, and remaining performance obligations reached $9 billion. Those figures suggest customers are expanding their commitments to the platform.
AI adoption is adding to Snowflake’s momentum. CoCo passed 9,100 accounts in the quarter, while CoWork expanded to 5,800 accounts. Executives called AI a “powerful flywheel” for consumption.
One concern surfaced on Snowflake’s September earnings call. The company cut its fiscal 2027 non-GAAP product gross margin guidance to 74% because fast-growing AI workloads carry a lower contribution margin. Then-CEO Sridhar Ramaswamy stated “As models have gotten more powerful, cost has absolutely become a concern.”
Cloudflare Steers Clear of the AI Capex Race
Cloudflare has taken a more selective path on AI spending, even as it restructures around what it calls an “agentic AI-first operating model.” On its Q2 2026 earnings call in August, then-CEO Matthew Prince explained why Cloudflare avoids selling commodity compute:
I think not all revenue is created equal. And if you’re selling what is just commodity compute, if you’re basically letting, you know, an AI company use your balance sheet and your credit rating in order to buy servers that are the same as everybody else’s servers, that’s just not attractive business for us.
Prince added that Cloudflare has “always focused on how we can squeeze as much out of every CapEx dollar as possible.” That sets Cloudflare apart from hyperscalers that buy servers and lease them back.
Yet, that discipline hasn’t insulated Cloudflare stock. Datadog has leaned into AI with launches such as Bits AI and AI Guard, and Datadog shares are doing slightly better, though still trailing the cloud ETF.
Snowflake’s Financing Question Hangs Over Cloud Names
Snowflake’s bull case rests on demand for data platforms that feed AI workloads, backed by three straight quarters of accelerating product revenue growth. Cloudflare bulls point to its capital discipline, and Datadog bulls to AI monitoring demand. The bear case for all three: investors keep marking down AI-linked names until financing concerns ease.
The next test for Snowflake is whether AI demand keeps product revenue growth on its guided path. Traders may want to check for whether SKYY closes its gap with QQQ.
Strong recent results give Snowflake, Cloudflare, and Datadog a fundamental buffer, while the financing concern could keep the three stocks volatile. Position sizes should be kept small, if you choose to invest at all, until the AI financing question resolves.

While media releases or rumors about a substantial change in a company's business prospects usually make its stock 'trending' and lead to an immediate price change, there are always some fundamental facts that eventually dominate the buy-and-hold decision-making.
Rather than focusing on anything else, we at Zacks prioritize evaluating the change in a company's earnings projection. This is because we believe the fair value for its stock is determined by the present value of its future stream of earnings.
Our analysis is essentially based on how sell-side analysts covering the stock are revising their earnings estimates to take the latest business trends into account. When earnings estimates for a company go up, the fair value for its stock goes up as well. And when a stock's fair value is higher than its current market price, investors tend to buy the stock, resulting in its price moving upward. At Goldman Sachs' Communacopia + Technology Conference on September 10, CFO David Obstler pointed to how little of the market has moved. He cited Datadog's customer announcements in banking, insurance, automotive, manufacturing, and airlines as evidence that migration is under way.
To catch those projects, salespeople in Datadog's key accounts group now cover one or two accounts "where the IT budget and conversion to the cloud can be in the tens of millions." Customers with $100,000 or more in annual recurring revenue reached about 4,720 at the end of the second quarter, up 23% from a year earlier. Obstler called these enterprise sales cycles very long, so that count tracks the strategy better than any single quarter's revenue.

November 4 shows whether AI-native customers keep moving onto Datadog, as Obstler described, or in-house, as Bernstein warned.
